decisions.choice: the last words of David: his final poem, placed among the closing chapters of Samuel
decisions.reason: Chapters 21-24 gather several pieces from David's reign outside the order of the story: David's song (chapter 22), these last words, the list of his warriors and the census. "Last" sets this poem near the end of his life, like Jacob's and Moses' final words (Genesis 49; Deuteronomy 33). The record of David's death comes later, in 1 Kings 2:1-10.

decisions.choice: oracle: a solemn utterance spoken under God's inspiration
decisions.reason: The word is used almost always of what God declares through a prophet ("declares the LORD"). Used of a man, it appears in Balaam's oracles, which begin in the same way: "oracle of Balaam son of Beor, and oracle of the man ..." (Numbers 24:3-4, 15-16). David's words are presented as prophecy, as verse 2 goes on to say.

decisions.choice: raised on high: lifted by God to a high position, as king
alternatives: the man raised up by the Most High
decisions.reason: The verb is passive: someone raised David up, and the next phrase shows it was God. The short word read as "on high" could also be a title of God, "the Most High", giving "the man raised up by the Most High". Either way, David's rise is God's doing.

decisions.choice: the pleasant one of the songs of Israel: the sweet singer of Israel's songs
alternatives: the darling of the Mighty One of Israel
decisions.reason: The phrase is short and its sense is uncertain. Taken with David's fame as a musician and poet (1 Samuel 16:18, 23; 2 Samuel 1:17; 22:1), it describes him as the one who made Israel's songs lovely. It can also mean "the favorite of Israel's songs", the hero its songs celebrate (1 Samuel 18:7), and the word for "songs" may instead mean "strength" or "protection", giving "the favorite of the Mighty One of Israel".

decisions.choice: the one anointed by the God of Jacob (Balanced); the king the God of Jacob anointed (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that the anointed one is the king, as it does for "the LORD's anointed" (1 Samuel 24:7). Readable also says "message" for "oracle", which is an uncommon word.

decisions.choice: "oracle" (L, B); "message" (R)

decisions.choice: tamko (L, B); ujumbe (R)

decisions.choice: the Rock of Israel: a title of God as Israel's firm protection
decisions.reason: A rock is a place of safety that does not move. God is called the Rock in David's song (22:2-3, 32, 47), in the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:4) and in Hannah's prayer (1 Samuel 2:2).

decisions.choice: one ruling ... righteous ... in the fear of God: a picture of the right kind of king, compared in verse 4 to the morning sun
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has two short phrases with no main verb: "a ruler over people, righteous; a ruler in the fear of God". The comparison that completes the thought comes in verse 4. The words describe what a king should be: just in dealing with people, and reverent toward God (Deuteronomy 17:18-20). David applies them to his own house in verse 5.

decisions.choice: God's words begin here and run to the end of verse 4
alternatives: God's words run to the end of verse 7
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has no quotation marks. "The God of Israel said ... to me" introduces what God said, and the picture of the righteous ruler in verses 3b-4 is that saying. In verse 5 David speaks again about his own house. Some take God's words to run on to the end of the poem.

decisions.choice: A king who rules
decisions.reason: Readable says "a king" for "one who rules", since the poem is about David's royal house. It says "deep respect" for "fear", which here means reverence, not terror.

decisions.choice: "les hommes" for humankind, without a gender span
decisions.reason: The English has no gender span here; French Balanced keeps "gouverner les hommes", a fixed expression in which "hommes" is plainly generic, while Literal says "les humains" and Readable "les gens".
